questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L2-Q01 · APPLY · D2 (proposed)
questions.stem:
Three branches are connected between the points A and B as shown in Fig. 1. The equivalent resistance between A and B is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 1: Three branches between A and B

hints.text: Trace paths sharing the same terminal nodes.
Check for uninterrupted series connections within each path.
Write the conductance sum using branch resistances.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: The circuit connects terminals A and B across three parallel branches between two common vertical busbars. Top branch: R_1 = 2 Ω. Middle branch: R_2 = 1 Ω and R_3 = 3 Ω in series. Bottom branch: R_4 = 4 Ω.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Resistors in series sum linearly: R_mid = R_2 + R_3 = 1 + 3 = 4 Ω. For three parallel branches sharing common potential difference V_AB, equivalent conductance is the sum of branch conductances: 1/R_AB = 1/R_top + 1/R_mid + 1/R_bot = 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/4.
3. Execution & Resolution: 1/R_AB = 2/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 4/4 = 1 Ω⁻¹. Inverting yields R_AB = 1.0 Ω. Matches Option A.
questions.check: Limiting sanity check: The equivalent resistance of parallel resistors must be strictly less than the smallest individual branch resistance (1 Ω < 2 Ω).

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L2-Q02 · APPLY · D2 (proposed)
questions.stem:
The equivalent resistance between A and B in the network of Fig. 2 is:
[FIG-stem-1]

hints.text: Find the first junction after terminal A.
Identify series elements inside each branch.
Write the equivalent of the parallel group, then account for the input resistor.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: The network consists of an input 2 Ω resistor in series with a parallel sub-network. The parallel sub-network has a top branch with 3 Ω and a bottom branch with 4 Ω and 2 Ω in series.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: In the parallel sub-network, the bottom branch resistance is R_bot = 4 + 2 = 6 Ω. The equivalent resistance of the parallel group is R_p = (R_top · R_bot)/(R_top + R_bot) = (3 · 6)/(3 + 6) = 18/9 = 2 Ω.
3. Execution & Resolution: The total resistance between A and B is the series sum: R_AB = R_series + R_p = 2 + 2 = 4 Ω. Matches Option B.
questions.check: Dimensional check: Summing [Ω] + [Ω] yields 4 Ω; R_p (2 Ω) is less than the smallest branch (3 Ω).

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L2-Q03 · MODEL · D2 (proposed)
questions.stem:
In the network of Fig. 3, a piece of ideal wire is connected across the 2 Ω resistor. The equivalent resistance between A and B is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 3: Wire connected across a resistor

hints.text: What potential difference can an ideal wire sustain?
Compare the bypassed resistor's terminals with the wire endpoints.
Redraw the remaining branches and write their equivalent resistance.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: The network consists of two main parallel branches between A and B: a top branch containing a 6 Ω resistor, and a bottom branch containing a 3 Ω resistor in series with a 2 Ω resistor that is bypassed by an ideal wire jumper.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: An ideal wire has resistance R = 0. In parallel with the 2 Ω resistor, the equivalent resistance of this section is R_parallel = (2 × 0)/(2 + 0) = 0 Ω. Hence, the 2 Ω resistor is completely bypassed (short-circuited), carrying zero current. The bottom branch resistance simplifies to R_bot = 3 + 0 = 3 Ω.
3. Execution & Resolution: The remaining circuit consists of the top branch (6 Ω) in parallel with the bottom branch (3 Ω): R_AB = (6 × 3)/(6 + 3) = 18/9 = 2 Ω. Matches Option C.
questions.check: Physical limit check: Without the shorting wire, R_bot would be 5 Ω and R_AB = 30/11 Ω ≈ 2.73 Ω. With the short circuit, equivalent resistance must decrease (2 Ω < 2.73 Ω), satisfying Rayleigh's monotonicity law.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L2-Q04 · MODEL · D2 (proposed)
questions.stem:
The equivalent resistance between A and B in the bridge network of Fig. 4 is:
[FIG-stem-1]

hints.text: Compare the two voltage dividers between A and B.
Use the condition for equal intermediate-node potentials.
Decide whether the central resistor carries current before reducing outer paths.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: The bridge consists of four outer arms: R_AC = 6 Ω, R_AD = 4 Ω, R_CB = 9 Ω, R_DB = 6 Ω, and a central bridge resistor R_CD = 10 Ω connected between intermediate nodes C and D.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Test the Wheatstone bridge balance condition: R_AC / R_AD = 6 / 4 = 3/2 = 1.5, and R_CB / R_DB = 9 / 6 = 3/2 = 1.5. Since R_AC / R_AD = R_CB / R_DB, the bridge is balanced. The electric potential at node C equals that at node D (V_C = V_D).

3. Execution & Resolution: Because V_C - V_D = 0, no current passes through the central 10 Ω resistor. Removing R_CD leaves two parallel branches: Branch ACB with R_ACB = 6 + 9 = 15 Ω, and Branch ADB with R_ADB = 4 + 6 = 10 Ω. The equivalent resistance is R_AB = (15 × 10)/(15 + 10) = 150/25 = 6 Ω. Matches Option B.
questions.check: Alternative check: Short-circuiting C and D (which is valid since V_C = V_D) gives R_AC||R_AD + R_CB||R_DB = (6×4)/(6+4) + (9×6)/(9+6) = 2.4 + 3.6 = 6.0 Ω.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L2-Q05 · SYNTHESIZE · D3 (proposed)
questions.stem:
The equivalent resistance between A and B in the bridge network of Fig. 5 is:
[FIG-stem-1]

hints.text: Compare ratios of the two voltage dividers.
For an unbalanced bridge choose nodal analysis or delta–star transformation.
Set up two KCL equations at C and D, or identify the triangle to transform.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: The bridge arms are R_AC = 2 Ω, R_AD = 6 Ω, R_CD = 4 Ω, R_CB = 6 Ω, and R_DB = 8 Ω. The bridge is unbalanced because 2/6 ≠ 6/8.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Convert the delta mesh formed by nodes A, C, D into an equivalent star connected to a neutral internal node N. The perimeter resistance sum is Σ R_Δ = 2 + 4 + 6 = 12 Ω. Using Kennelly's Delta-to-Star formula: R_A = (R_AC · R_AD)/Σ = (2 × 6)/12 = 1.0 Ω; R_C = (R_AC · R_CD)/Σ = (2 × 4)/12 = 8/12 = 2/3 Ω; R_D = (R_AD · R_CD)/Σ = (6 × 4)/12 = 24/12 = 2.0 Ω.

3. Execution & Resolution: From node N, the circuit splits into two parallel branches terminating at B: Branch 1 through C: R_C + R_CB = 2/3 + 6 = 20/3 Ω. Branch 2 through D: R_D + R_DB = 2 + 8 = 10 Ω. Parallel combination between N and B: R_NB = ((20/3) × 10) / (20/3 + 10) = (200/3) / (50/3) = 200/50 = 4.0 Ω. Total equivalent resistance: R_AB = R_A + R_NB = 1.0 + 4.0 = 5.0 Ω. Matches Option C.
questions.check: Nodal analysis verification: Let V_A = 5V, V_B = 0V. KCL at C: (V_C-5)/2 + (V_C-V_D)/4 + V_C/6 = 0 => 11 V_C - 3 V_D = 30. KCL at D: (V_D-5)/6 + (V_D-V_C)/4 + V_D/8 = 0 => -6 V_C + 13 V_D = 20. Solving yields V_C = 3.6 V, V_D = 3.2 V. Total current I = (5-3.6)/2 + (5-3.2)/6 = 0.7 + 0.3 = 1.0 A. Hence R_AB = V/I = 5/1 = 5.0 Ω.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L2-Q06 · MODEL · D2 (proposed)
questions.stem:
In the network of Fig. 6, the equivalent resistance between A and B when the switch S is open and when S is closed are respectively:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 6: Bridge network with a switch

hints.text: Draw the networks for S open and closed separately.
An ideal closed switch merges endpoint potentials.
For each state identify series and parallel groups.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: The circuit has four resistors: R_AC = 6 Ω, R_CB = 12 Ω, R_AD = 12 Ω, R_DB = 6 Ω. A switch S connects node C to node D.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: State 1 (S is OPEN): There is zero conducting path between C and D. Branch ACB has R_ACB = 6 + 12 = 18 Ω. Branch ADB has R_ADB = 12 + 6 = 18 Ω. R_open = (18 × 18)/(18 + 18) = 18/2 = 9 Ω.

3. Execution & Resolution: State 2 (S is CLOSED): Nodes C and D are short-circuited together (V_C = V_D). Resistors R_AC (6 Ω) and R_AD (12 Ω) are in parallel across nodes A and CD: R_left = (6 × 12)/(6 + 12) = 72/18 = 4 Ω. Resistors R_CB (12 Ω) and R_DB (6 Ω) are in parallel across nodes CD and B: R_right = (12 × 6)/(12 + 6) = 72/18 = 4 Ω. Total resistance is R_closed = R_left + R_right = 4 + 4 = 8 Ω. The respective values are 9 Ω and 8 Ω. Matches Option B.
questions.check: Sanity check: Closing an internal switch provides additional conduction pathways; by Rayleigh's Monotonicity Law, R_closed must be strictly less than or equal to R_open (8 Ω < 9 Ω).

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L2-Q07 · APPLY · D2 (proposed)
questions.stem:
Six identical resistors, each of 6 Ω, are joined to form a regular hexagon as shown in Fig. 7. The equivalent resistance between the adjacent corners A and B is:
[FIG-stem-1]

hints.text: Trace both routes around the hexagon from A to B.
Resistors along uninterrupted paths are in series.
Write the parallel equivalent of both complete paths.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: A regular closed hexagon consists of N = 6 equal resistors of resistance R = 6 Ω each. Terminals A and B are adjacent vertices.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: The closed perimeter divides into two parallel branches connecting A and B: Branch 1 is the single adjacent side AB, with R_1 = 6 Ω. Branch 2 is the perimeter path traversing the other 5 sides in series: R_2 = 5 × 6 = 30 Ω.
3. Execution & Resolution: The equivalent resistance between A and B is given by the parallel formula: R_AB = (R_1 · R_2)/(R_1 + R_2) = (6 × 30)/(6 + 30) = 180/36 = 5.0 Ω. Matches Option C.
questions.check: General formula check: For an n-sided regular polygon with edge r across adjacent corners, R_adj = (n - 1)r / n. Here n = 6, r = 6 Ω => R = (5/6) × 6 = 5 Ω.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L2-Q08 · APPLY · D2 (proposed)
questions.stem:
Five resistors, each of 6 Ω, are connected as shown in Fig. 8: four form the sides of a square ABCD and one forms the diagonal AC. The equivalent resistance between A and C is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 8: Square with a diagonal resistor

hints.text: Trace independent routes from A to C.
Paths between identical nodes have the same voltage.
Find each path resistance before adding conductances.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: The network consists of 5 identical resistors of R = 6 Ω. Four resistors form the square perimeter (AB, BC, CD, DA) and the fifth lies along diagonal AC. Terminals are placed at opposite corners A and C.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Between nodes A and C, there are three parallel pathways: Branch 1 along the top perimeter ADC: R_ADC = R_AD + R_DC = 6 + 6 = 12 Ω. Branch 2 along the bottom perimeter ABC: R_ABC = R_AB + R_BC = 6 + 6 = 12 Ω. Branch 3 directly through the diagonal AC: R_diag = 6 Ω.

3. Execution & Resolution: The equivalent resistance R_AC is given by: 1/R_AC = 1/R_ADC + 1/R_ABC + 1/R_diag = 1/12 + 1/12 + 1/6 = 2/12 + 1/6 = 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6 = 1/3 Ω⁻¹. Inverting gives R_AC = 3.0 Ω. Matches Option B.
questions.check: Symmetry check: By symmetry across diagonal AC, branch ADC and branch ABC have equal current. Since both are 12 Ω, their parallel combination is 6 Ω. In parallel with diagonal 6 Ω: 6||6 = 3 Ω.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L2-Q09 · MODEL · D2 (proposed)
questions.stem:
For the same network of Fig. 8 (all five resistors of 6 Ω), the equivalent resistance between the corners B and D is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 8: Square with a diagonal resistor

hints.text: Use B and D as the terminals.
Identify a reflection fixing both terminals.
Infer potential equality and decide whether the diagonal carries current.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: The 5-resistor network has each resistor equal to R = 6 Ω. Terminals are now corners B and D. Diagonal resistor AC bridges the two opposite non-terminal corners A and C.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Apply mirror symmetry across the axis line BD. The upper half (BCD) and lower half (BAD) are identical mirror images. Therefore, the electric potential at corner A must equal the potential at corner C: V_A = V_C. The potential difference across the diagonal resistor is ΔV_AC = V_A - V_C = 0.

3. Execution & Resolution: Because ΔV_AC = 0, zero current flows through the diagonal resistor AC. It can be removed from the circuit without disturbing node potentials or branch currents. The remaining network consists of two parallel branches: Branch BAD with R_BAD = R_BA + R_AD = 6 + 6 = 12 Ω, and Branch BCD with R_BCD = R_BC + R_CD = 6 + 6 = 12 Ω. Equivalent resistance between B and D is R_BD = (12 × 12)/(12 + 12) = 12/2 = 6.0 Ω. Matches Option C.
questions.check: Bridge perspective check: Viewing B and D as input/output terminals, the circuit forms a symmetric Wheatstone bridge with ratio R_BA/R_AD = 6/6 = 1 and R_BC/R_CD = 6/6 = 1. Since the bridge is balanced, the bridge resistor AC carries 0 A.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L2-Q10 · SYNTHESIZE · D3 (proposed)
questions.stem:
A square ABCD of four 6 Ω resistors has its centre O joined to each corner by a 6 Ω resistor, as shown in Fig. 9. The equivalent resistance between the opposite corners A and C is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 9: Square with spokes to the centre

hints.text: Mark terminal potentials and inspect symmetry.
Find a reflection fixing A and C and a symmetry interchanging them.
Identify equal-potential vertices before reducing the branches.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: The network consists of 8 equal resistors of R = 6 Ω: four outer perimeter resistors (AB, BC, CD, DA) and four spoke resistors (OA, OB, OC, OD). Terminals are at opposite diagonal corners A and C.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Apply reflection and inversion symmetry. Let terminal A be at potential V_A = V and terminal C at V_C = 0. The perpendicular bisector plane passes through vertices B, D and centre O. By bilateral symmetry across AC, V_B = V_D. By potential inversion symmetry from A to C, the potential at the midpoint O is V_O = V/2, and the potentials at B and D are V_B = V_D = V/2.

3. Execution & Resolution: Because V_B = V_O = V_D = V/2, the potential difference across spoke OB is V_B - V_O = 0, and across spoke OD is V_D - V_O = 0. Neither spoke carries current, so both resistors OB and OD can be removed. The remaining circuit between A and C consists of three parallel branches: Branch 1 (outer top): ADC with R_1 = 6 + 6 = 12 Ω. Branch 2 (outer bottom): ABC with R_2 = 6 + 6 = 12 Ω. Branch 3 (inner diagonal): AOC with R_3 = 6 + 6 = 12 Ω. Combining the three 12 Ω branches in parallel: 1/R_AC = 1/12 + 1/12 + 1/12 = 3/12 = 1/4 Ω⁻¹. Therefore, R_AC = 4.0 Ω. Matches Option D.
questions.check: Independent nodal check: set V_A=1, V_C=0. Reflection and terminal interchange give V_B=V_D=V_O=1/2. The three edges leaving A each carry 1/(2r), so R_eq=2r/3=4 Ω.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L2-Q11 · SYNTHESIZE · D3 (proposed)
questions.stem:
Twelve identical resistors, each of 4 Ω, form the 2 × 2 square grid of Fig. 10. The equivalent resistance between the opposite corners A and B is:
[FIG-stem-1]

hints.text: Identify both diagonals and all nine nodes.
Set terminal potentials to 1 and 0; use reflection and terminal interchange.
Write KCL at a node adjacent to A after grouping equipotential vertices.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Set V_A=1 V and V_B=0 V. Label grid nodes (i,j), i,j=0,1,2, with A=(0,0), B=(2,2). Each edge has resistance r=4 Ω.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Reflection about AB gives V(1,0)=V(0,1)=x. Reflection interchanging A and B gives V(2,0)=V(1,1)=V(0,2)=1/2 and V(2,1)=V(1,2)=1−x. KCL at (1,0): (x−1)+(x−1/2)+(x−1/2)=0, so x=2/3.
3. Execution & Resolution: The two edges leaving A each carry (1−2/3)/r A. Thus I=2/(3r) and R_AB=3r/2=6 Ω, option C.
questions.check: KCL at all three midline nodes is satisfied since neighbors pair at x and 1−x. The input current leaves A through just two edges.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L2-Q12 · APPLY · D2 (proposed)
questions.stem:
A uniform wire of total resistance 18 Ω is bent into an equilateral triangle ABC, and M is the mid-point of side BC, as shown in Fig. 11. The equivalent resistance between A and M is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 11: Uniform wire bent into a triangle

hints.text: Translate side lengths into resistance.
M divides BC into equal lengths.
Trace both complete routes from A to M; combine them.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: A uniform wire of total resistance R_total = 18 Ω forms equilateral triangle ABC. Each side has resistance R_side = 18/3 = 6 Ω. Midpoint M divides side BC into two equal halves: R_BM = R_MC = 3 Ω.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: The median AM is a line of bilateral symmetry. Two distinct paths connect terminal A to terminal M: Path 1 through vertex B: R_1 = R_AB + R_BM = 6 + 3 = 9 Ω. Path 2 through vertex C: R_2 = R_AC + R_MC = 6 + 3 = 9 Ω.
3. Execution & Resolution: The two paths operate in parallel between A and M: R_AM = (R_1 · R_2)/(R_1 + R_2) = (9 × 9)/(9 + 9) = 81/18 = 4.5 Ω. Matches Option D.
questions.check: Symmetry check: Two equal 9 Ω branches in parallel give half their value: 9/2 = 4.5 Ω.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L2-Q13 · APPLY · D2 (proposed)
questions.stem:
A uniform wire of resistance 24 Ω is bent into a circular ring, and a straight wire of resistance 12 Ω is joined along a diameter PQ, as shown in Fig. 12. The equivalent resistance between P and Q is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 12: Ring with a diametral wire

hints.text: Identify both arcs and the diametral path.
Uniform wire resistance is proportional to arc length.
Write a conductance sum for the paths between P and Q.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: A circular ring has total perimeter resistance R_ring = 24 Ω. A straight diameter PQ has resistance R_diam = 12 Ω. Terminals are situated at endpoints P and Q.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Diameter PQ divides the circular ring into two equal semicircular branches in parallel with the diametral conductor: Top semicircle: R_top = 24/2 = 12 Ω. Bottom semicircle: R_bot = 24/2 = 12 Ω. Diameter wire: R_diam = 12 Ω.

3. Execution & Resolution: All three branches share nodes P and Q and operate in parallel: 1/R_PQ = 1/R_top + 1/R_diam + 1/R_bot = 1/12 + 1/12 + 1/12 = 3/12 = 1/4 Ω⁻¹. Inverting gives R_PQ = 12/3 = 4.0 Ω. Matches Option A.
questions.check: Parallel reduction check: Three equal resistors of 12 Ω in parallel yield R = 12/3 = 4 Ω.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L2-Q14 · SYNTHESIZE · D4 (proposed)
questions.stem:
Twelve identical resistors, each of 12 Ω, form the edges of a cube. The equivalent resistance between the ends A and B of one edge, as shown in Fig. 13, is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 13: Cube of resistors, terminals at the ends of an edge

hints.text: Label all eight vertices; set A to 1 V and B to 0 V.
Find a symmetry fixing A and B and one interchanging them.
Write KCL for independent node groups and find total input current.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Use cube coordinates A=(0,0,0), B=(1,0,0) with equal resistance r. Apply 1 V to A and 0 V to B. The symmetry exchanging y and z fixes both terminals.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Let V(0,1,0)=V(0,0,1)=x and V(0,1,1)=y. Terminal-interchange symmetry gives V(1,1,0)=V(1,0,1)=1−x and V(1,1,1)=1−y. KCL at x gives (x−1)+(x−y)+(x−(1−x))=0, i.e. 4x−y=2. At y, 2(y−x)+(y−(1−y))=0, i.e. 4y−2x=1.
3. Execution & Resolution: Solve x=9/14, y=4/7. Input current I=[1+2(1−x)]/r=12/(7r). Therefore R_AB=7r/12=7 Ω, option D.
questions.check: Direct edge carries 1/r A, other two incident edges each carry 5/(14r) A. Total 12/(7r); equivalent resistance is below r.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L2-Q15 · SYNTHESIZE · D4 (proposed)
questions.stem:
Twelve identical resistors, each of 8 Ω, form the edges of a cube. The equivalent resistance between the ends A and B of a face diagonal, as shown in Fig. 14, is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 14: Cube of resistors, terminals at the ends of a face diagonal

hints.text: Label the terminal face and the opposite face.
Use reflection fixing A and B and the symmetry interchanging them.
Set A to 1 V and B to 0 V; write KCL for unresolved opposite-face potentials.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Label A=(0,0,0), B=(1,1,0), set their potentials to 1 and 0 V, and let r=8 Ω. Other two vertices on the terminal face have potential 1/2 by reflection and terminal interchange.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: On opposite face z=1, nodes (1,0,1) and (0,1,1) also have potential 1/2. Let V(0,0,1)=x, V(1,1,1)=1−x. KCL at (0,0,1): (x−1)+2(x−1/2)=0, giving x=2/3.
3. Execution & Resolution: The three edges leaving A carry [1/2+1/2+(1−2/3)]/r=4/(3r) A. Thus R_AB=3r/4=6 Ω, option B.
questions.check: Five distinct potentials are 0, 1/3, 1/2, 2/3 and 1 V. The result is less than r and exceeds the adjacent-edge result 7r/12.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L2-Q16 · MODEL · D2 (proposed)
questions.stem:
Six identical resistors, each of 10 Ω, form the edges of a tetrahedron ABCD, as shown in Fig. 15. The equivalent resistance between the corners A and B is:
[FIG-stem-1]

hints.text: List the six edges of the tetrahedron.
Which vertex exchange fixes both terminals?
Infer which edge has zero voltage before reducing the remaining network.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Six identical resistors of r = 10 Ω form the 6 edges of regular tetrahedron ABCD (AB, AC, AD, BC, BD, CD). External terminals are corners A and B.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Notice that vertices C and D are symmetrically situated with respect to both terminal A and terminal B (d(A,C) = d(A,D) = r, and d(B,C) = d(B,D) = r). By symmetry, V_C = V_D. Since the potential difference across edge CD is zero, resistor CD carries no current and can be removed.

3. Execution & Resolution: The remaining circuit between A and B consists of three parallel branches: Branch 1: direct edge AB with R_AB = r = 10 Ω. Branch 2: path ACB with R_ACB = r + r = 2r = 20 Ω. Branch 3: path ADB with R_ADB = r + r = 2r = 20 Ω. Combining in parallel: 1/R_eq = 1/r + 1/(2r) + 1/(2r) = 1/r + 1/r = 2/r. Hence, R_eq = r/2 = 10/2 = 5.0 Ω. Matches Option A.
questions.check: Tetrahedron topological invariance: Because all 4 vertices of a regular tetrahedron are mutually symmetric, the equivalent resistance between ANY pair of vertices is identically r/2 = 5 Ω.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L2-Q17 · APPLY · D2 (proposed)
questions.stem:
All the resistors in the ladder network of Fig. 16 are 8 Ω. The equivalent resistance between A and B is:
[FIG-stem-1]

hints.text: Start with the rightmost termination.
Identify a series pair and shunt after each reduction.
Repeat right to left until reaching A and B.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: The network is a 3-section finite ladder. Every resistor is R = 8 Ω. Terminals A and B are at the left input port.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Collapse the ladder sequentially from right to left: Section 3 (far right): The terminating 8 Ω series resistor and 8 Ω shunt resistor form a series branch: R_s3 = 8 + 8 = 16 Ω. This 16 Ω is in parallel with the second shunt resistor (8 Ω): R_p2 = (16 × 8)/(16 + 8) = 128/24 = 16/3 Ω.

3. Execution & Resolution: Add the middle 8 Ω series resistor: R_s2 = 8 + 16/3 = 40/3 Ω. This 40/3 Ω is in parallel with the first shunt resistor (8 Ω): R_p1 = ((40/3) × 8) / (40/3 + 8) = (320/3) / (64/3) = 320/64 = 5.0 Ω. Finally, add the first input series resistor (8 Ω): R_AB = 8 + R_p1 = 8 + 5 = 13.0 Ω. Matches Option A.
questions.check: Bounds check: Total resistance must be greater than the first series resistor (13 Ω > 8 Ω) and less than all series resistors combined (13 Ω < 24 Ω).

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L2-Q18 · MODEL · D3 (proposed)
questions.stem:
The ladder network of Fig. 17 continues indefinitely, each section having a 4 Ω series resistor and a 3 Ω shunt resistor. The equivalent resistance between A and B is:
[FIG-stem-1]

hints.text: What is unchanged if the first repeating section is removed?
Assign the same unknown resistance to the whole ladder and identical tail.
Identify series and parallel connections in the first section; construct a self-consistency equation.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: The ladder extends to infinity, with identical repeating unit cells having series resistance R_s = 4 Ω and shunt resistance R_p = 3 Ω. Let R_AB = R be the driving point resistance between input terminals A and B.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Due to infinite self-similarity, the entire sub-ladder to the right of the first shunt resistor has equivalent resistance equal to R. Thus, the circuit simplifies to a 4 Ω resistor in series with the parallel combination of a 3 Ω resistor and R: R = 4 + (3R)/(3 + R).

3. Execution & Resolution: Multiply through by (3 + R): R(3 + R) = 4(3 + R) + 3R => 3R + R² = 12 + 4R + 3R => R² - 4R - 12 = 0. Factor the quadratic: (R - 6)(R + 2) = 0. Since physical electrical resistance must be positive (R > 0), we reject R = -2 Ω and obtain R = 6.0 Ω. Matches Option D.
questions.check: Convergence check: Truncating after 1 stage: 4 + 3 = 7 Ω. After 2 stages: 4 + (3×7)/10 = 6.1 Ω. After 3 stages: 4 + (3×6.1)/9.1 = 6.01 Ω -> converges monotonically to 6.0 Ω.

questions.stem: Three resistors of 6 Ω each are used, all three in every arrangement, in any series and/or parallel combination. Which one of the following values of equivalent resistance CANNOT be obtained?

hints.text: All three resistors must be used.
Enumerate configurations by whether the outermost connection is series or parallel.
Calculate each distinct topology's resistance and compare choices.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Three identical resistors of R = 6 Ω are combined using all three elements in each arrangement. We seek the value that cannot be realized.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Enumerate all four possible topological combinations of 3 identical resistors: Case 1 (All three in series): R_eq = R + R + R = 3R = 3 × 6 = 18 Ω. Case 2 (All three in parallel): 1/R_eq = 1/R + 1/R + 1/R = 3/R => R_eq = R/3 = 6/3 = 2 Ω (Option B is obtainable). Case 3 (Two in parallel, in series with the third): R_eq = (R || R) + R = 3 + 6 = 9 Ω (Option D is obtainable). Case 4 (Two in series, in parallel with the third): R_eq = (R + R) || R = 12 || 6 = (12 × 6)/(12 + 6) = 72/18 = 4 Ω (Option C is obtainable).

3. Execution & Resolution: The complete set of achievable equivalent resistances is {2 Ω, 4 Ω, 9 Ω, 18 Ω}. The value 12 Ω is absent from this set (12 Ω would require only two 6 Ω resistors in series, but all three must be used). Therefore, 12 Ω CANNOT be obtained. Matches Option A.
questions.check: The outermost series or parallel connection partitions three identical resistors into one resistor and a two-resistor group. The latter is either series or parallel, giving four exhaustive resistance values.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is/are correct? [One or more options may be correct.]
options: A: Removing (open-circuiting) one resistor from a network can decrease the equivalent resistance between the terminals.
B: Two resistors connected in parallel can have an equivalent resistance greater than the larger of the two.
C: Connecting an extra resistor in parallel across any two points of a network cannot increase the equivalent resistance between the terminals of the network.
D: Replacing one resistor of a network by an ideal wire (short-circuiting it) cannot increase the equivalent resistance between the terminals of the network.
questions.answer: C, D: Connecting an extra resistor in parallel across any two points of a network cannot increase the equivalent resistance between the terminals of the network; Replacing one resistor of a network by an ideal wire (short-circuiting it) cannot increase the equivalent resistance between the terminals of the network

hints.text: Assume a connected passive network of positive resistors.
Consider minimum dissipation at fixed terminal current.
For each change, decide how available current paths change; test the simple parallel claim separately.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Consider a passive connected network of positive ohmic resistors driven by fixed terminal current I. For any conserving current distribution, dissipation is P=Σ r_k i_k².

2. Physical Model & Formulation: The physical distribution minimizes P subject to charge conservation. Adding a branch permits the old distribution with zero current in the new branch; minimum P cannot increase. Shorting a resistor lowers its resistance, so the old trial distribution dissipates no more power. Removing a branch restricts allowed distributions, so minimum P cannot decrease.

3. Execution & Resolution: A is false because removing a branch cannot decrease resistance. B is false since R_parallel=R₁R₂/(R₁+R₂) is less than either positive resistance. C and D are true by minimum dissipation; at fixed I, P=I²R_eq.
questions.check: Equality can occur if a modified branch carries zero current or joins equipotential nodes. Removing a branch may also disconnect the terminals, making resistance infinite.
